If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

Step-by-step diagnosis:

1. The current failing test testStop3() asserts that when parsing the command line with stopAtNonOption=true, tokens after a non-option are treated as extra arguments. The test expects exactly 3 extra arguments from the input: "--zop==1", "-abtoast", and "--b=bar".

2. The current bug report explains that PosixParser does not stop processing tokens correctly when encountering an unrecognized long option (like "--zop"). Instead, it "bursts" or splits tokens around '=', processes them further, and splits combined short options, instead of stopping as expected with stopAtNonOption enabled.

3. A relevant code snippet is from PosixParser.burstToken(String token, boolean stopAtNonOption), which processes tokens character by character, breaking combined short options into separate tokens and handling option arguments.

4. In the burstToken method, the option characters are checked one by one. If the character is recognized as an option (options.hasOption(ch)), it is processed as such. If not recognized and stopAtNonOption=true, it calls process(token.substring(i)) to handle the rest of the token differently, then breaks. If stopAtNonOption=false, it adds the whole token as-is and breaks.

5. The problem seems to be the handling of unrecognized long options. According to the bug report, even with stopAtNonOption=true, tokens after such an unrecognized long option are still burst and split erroneously, instead of being preserved as extra arguments.

6. The test expects "3 extra args" indicating that the token "--zop==1" (unrecognized long option) and subsequent tokens are kept intact in the argument list. But the parser instead splits "--zop==1" into tokens, breaking "=" and processing further, causing the test failure.

7. Recent bug reports reinforce this diagnosis by noting that the PosixParser's bursting process continues after a non-option character is found even if stopAtNonOption is enabled, causing similar issues.

8. The root cause appears to be in the bursting and processing logic when handling unrecognized options with stopAtNonOption=true. Specifically, the parser fails to stop token bursting and preserve the remainder tokens intact after encountering a non-recognized option. The implementation allows further token splitting and processing instead.

In summary, the test failure and bug report indicate that PosixParser incorrectly continues bursting and splitting tokens after a non recognized long option, when stopAtNonOption is enabled. The burstToken method tries to handle this but is flawed in this scenario, causing the parser to process tokens that should be preserved as extra arguments instead. This mismatch in expected vs actual token treatment causes the test failure. The solution likely involves correcting the bursting logic to appropriately stop token processing and preserve tokens following unrecognized long options when stopAtNonOption is true.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
